figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overall architecture of PMS-SR. All attention runs on the LR grid (blue). Stage 1 (orange) expands the features $\times 2\!\to\!\times 4\!\to\!\times 8$ with decreasing widths; the $\times 2$ output is a residual over the bicubically upsampled input, and each higher scale is a residual over the detached, bicubically upsampled prediction of the previous scale (dashed cascade). Stage 2, the IMR module (red, Fig. 3), refines all scales jointly; the heads of both stages are green. The bottom row shows the actual input and outputs of one forward pass at their true relative sizes.
figures.headline: All attention runs on the low-resolution grid, with a progressive cascade stage followed by a joint refinement stage.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 1, the model comprises (i) an LR-grid CSWin backbone, (ii) a Stage-1 progressive reconstruction pyramid with cascaded anchors, and (iii) the Stage-2 inter-scale mutual refinement (IMR) module.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: One CSWin block of PMS-SR (Eqs. (3)–(5)): two parallel stripe attentions (horizontal and vertical, half the channels each) plus a channel attention block (CAB) scaled by a learnable $\alpha$, followed by a LeFF feed-forward network. Blue boxes are adopted from prior work without structural change: stripe attention with LePE [14], the CAB of HAT [8], and LeFF [34]. The learnable $\alpha$ and the single-precision attention logits are annotated.
figures.headline: Each attention block runs horizontal and vertical stripe attention alongside a channel attention branch, followed by a feed-forward network.
citing_sentences: where $X_{l-1}$ and $X_{l}$ are the input and output of the $l$-th block, $\mathrm{Attn}_{h}$ and $\mathrm{Attn}_{v}$ are the horizontal- and vertical-stripe multi-head self-attentions (H- and V-stripe MSA in Fig. 2), $\|$ denotes channel concatenation, $\mathrm{Proj}$ is a linear projection, and LeFF [34] is a feed-forward network with an interleaved $3{\times}3$ depthwise convolution for locality.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The inter-scale mutual refinement (IMR) module, Stage 2 (Eqs. (10)–(12)). Fine features are folded back by space-to-depth ($\mathrm{PU}_{\downarrow r}$), coarse features are aligned to the finer grid by deformable alignment ($\mathrm{DA}_{s}$), and the streams are fused per pixel ($\mathrm{SCF}_{s}$). The $\times 8$ row refines entirely on the $\times 4$ grid and expands only the correction (refine-then-upsample). All refinements are residual.
figures.headline: The refinement module folds fine features to coarser grids, aligns coarse features to finer grids, and fuses the streams per pixel.

At $\times 8$, PMS-SR is ahead of the best baseline by 0.39 dB on the BSD100 violinist, 1.45 and 0.65 dB on the two Urban100 façades, and 0.51 dB on the Manga109 title in Fig. 4.

citing_sentences: Fig. 7 summarizes the trade-off at $\times 8$: PMS-SR reaches the five-benchmark mean of SwinIR-M, DBPN-RES-MR64-3, and RDRN (25.37 vs. 25.35–25.38 dB) with at most 22% of the parameters of their three-model ladders.

abstract: Super-resolution networks are trained for one magnification factor, so several output resolutions require several models. We propose PMS-SR, a progressive single-input multiple-output network that produces $\times 2$, $\times 4$, and $\times 8$ results in one forward pass, with a Transformer backbone on the low-resolution grid. In Stage 1, each scale is predicted as a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous scale’s prediction. With Dirac and zero initialization, training starts exactly from the bicubic cascade, and each head adds only the band the previous scale lacks. In Stage 2, inter-scale mutual refinement couples the scales in both directions through space-to-depth feedback, deformable alignment, and per-pixel fusion, so $\times 8$ features refine the $\times 2$ output. Trained on DF2K, the 7.95M-parameter model achieves a higher PSNR than every compared multi-scale method at $\times 4$ and $\times 8$ on all five standard benchmarks. At $\times 8$, it outperforms the $\times 8$-specific DRN-L on all of them, leads all compared methods on Urban100, and is within 0.13 dB of the best result elsewhere. Against three single-scale SwinIR-M models, PMS-SR uses 22% of the parameters, runs $2.9\times$ faster on BSD100 inputs, and its outputs agree 6.7–12.4 dB more closely. Code and pretrained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/PMS-SR upon acceptance.

sections.body: Adaptive streaming, zoomable playback and surveillance need several renditions of the same content, and single-scale models need one large network for each. The paper proposes PMS-SR, which produces ×2, ×4 and ×8 outputs in one forward pass, with all attention on the low-resolution grid. It lists three contributions: a single 7.95M-parameter model, cascaded residual anchoring, and inter-scale mutual refinement. In the ablation, replacing the cascade with a direct anchor costs 2.4 dB at ×8 on BSD100. On the five benchmarks, PMS-SR has the highest PSNR among the compared multi-scale methods at ×4 and ×8. At ×8 it is at least 0.16 dB ahead on Urban100 and at most 0.13 dB behind elsewhere. Its three renditions agree 6.7–12.4 dB more closely than those of three independently trained models.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Multi-scale delivery usually needs one model per factor, so the paper trains one network for ×2, ×4 and ×8.

sections.body: The section groups prior work into CNN-based, Transformer and state-space single-scale models, progressive multi-scale methods, and feature alignment. LapSRN, MS-LapSRN, MSWSR, MLWAN and ProSR-L output several scales with convolutional or wavelet-based designs. Fine-to-coarse feedback appears in D-DBPN, SRFBN and DRN, but each of these delivers one factor only. The paper states three differences from the multi-scale methods: its stripe-window Transformer runs only on the low-resolution grid, its anchors form a bicubic cascade over predicted images, and a second stage couples the scales in both directions. It also notes that ProSR reports anchoring on previous outputs can destabilize training, and keeps that anchor while blocking gradients from higher scales.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing progressive multi-scale methods pass information only from coarse to fine scales.

sections.body: PMS-SR takes one low-resolution input and outputs six images in a single pass: Stage-1 and Stage-2 predictions for ×2, ×4 and ×8. The backbone is a shallow extractor followed by four residual groups of four stripe-attention blocks, all on the low-resolution grid. Each block adds a channel attention branch that the paper takes from HAT, with a learnable scale. In Stage 1, each higher-scale head predicts a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous prediction. The skip convolutions are Dirac-initialized and the last layer of each head is zero-initialized, so training starts exactly from the bicubic cascade. A direct anchor would start within 0.03 dB of this point. Stage 2 applies space-to-depth feedback, deformable alignment and per-pixel fusion, and the ×8 refinement runs on the ×4 grid. The loss weights the scales as 0.5, 0.8 and 1.2.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each scale is a residual over a detached bicubic cascade, and a second stage then refines all scales jointly.

sections.body: Training uses DF2K, with 48×48 low-resolution patches, for 300k iterations at batch size 16. Training takes about 146 GPU-hours on one RTX 4090. Evaluation uses Y-channel PSNR and SSIM on Set5, Set14, BSD100, Urban100 and Manga109, with a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Holm adjustment. Tiled inference changes PSNR by at most 0.04 dB at ×8 compared with whole-image inference. Whole-image inference for all three outputs needs 142.17 GFLOPs, against 159.15 GFLOPs for the three-model SwinIR-M ladder. One whole-image pass takes 32.8 ms, against 94.4 ms for the ladder, a 2.9× speed-up. Cross-scale agreement reaches 45.6–52.4 dB for ×8 to ×4, against 34.5–42.5 dB for three independent SwinIR-M models.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: PMS-SR has the highest PSNR among compared multi-scale methods in every ×4 and ×8 entry.

sections.body: The discussion attributes the affordable ×8 output to LR-grid feature extraction with a narrowing channel pyramid, detached cascaded anchors, and bidirectional IMR coupling. It presents the single-pass design for edge nodes, which would otherwise run three SwinIR-M-class models with 4.5× the parameters. Its limitations are stated as three points. At ×2, single-scale Transformers remain 0.2–1.8 dB ahead, and the loss weights and bicubic targets may contribute. The sub-pixel pyramid restricts factors to powers of two, so non-dyadic factors need an extra branch. The experiments use only bicubic degradation, and temporal consistency is not modeled, so per-frame application can still flicker.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The discussion credits three design choices for affordable ×8 and flags weaker ×2 accuracy and no temporal modeling.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution as the coupling between renditions rather than the backbone, which is described as deliberately standard. Cascaded anchors start optimization from the bicubic cascade, and inter-scale mutual refinement exchanges information in both directions. The paper reports the highest PSNR among compared multi-scale methods at ×4 and ×8, an advantage over DRN-L at ×8 on all five benchmarks, and a margin within 0.13 dB of the strongest ×8-specific models elsewhere. Future work includes curriculum-style scale scheduling, extension to arbitrary factors, and application of the cascaded anchors and refinement to video super-resolution and joint restoration.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A single pass of one 7.95M-parameter model delivers ×2, ×4 and ×8 with 22% of a three-model ladder's parameters.
